basis: No contemporary leg found. Searched OR III-1 for every Morton item: his telegrams of 17 and 19 and 20 April 1861 (OR III-1 pp 80 and 89) show Morton pressing Cameron ('Why has there been so much delay in sending arms?' OR III-1 p89, 19 April 1861) but that is boldness and is already carried by the boldness cell, not evidence of holding firm under pressure. Rebellion Record vol 1 holds no Morton document. Foulke (a 1899 life) narrates his calming the 1861 three-months men (p127) but is a later narrative. Not reached: the Indiana Documentary Journal 1861 and the text of the Six Regiment Act (7 May 1861) that retroactively covered what Foulke says he did 'upon his own responsibility'. The Appletons nerve rests on the 1863-65 extra-legal finance, which is after the 31 July 1861 limit.

Morton's address of welcome to President-elect Lincoln at Indianapolis, 11 Feb 1861, printed verbatim by Foulke (a later work printing the document: only the speech's words count): 'it will be the duty of all good citizens, without distinction of party, to yield a cordial and earnest support to every measure of your administration calculated to maintain the Union' (Foulke p107, OCR of the running head lost the page number so p107 is inferred from the p108 head). A public welcome by the governor who had just taken office, so it supports above and cannot support high. Foulke is a secondary work, the speech is the contemporary document.

basis: Two documents of Morton's own, both before 5 March 1861. (1) On 1 Feb 1861, before naming Indiana's commissioners to the Peace Congress, he put four written questions to each, printed verbatim in Foulke p105: 'Would you favor any proposition of compromise that involves an amendment of the constitution of the United States?' and 'Are you in favor of maintaining the constitution of the United States as it is, and of enforcing the laws?' (he kept the written answers to hold them to it, Foulke p106). (2) Letter to the Secretary of War, Indianapolis 17 Jan 1861, OR III-1 p41: 'I write for the purpose of obtaining information as to the quantity and kind of arms to which the State of Indiana is entitled', two months before any call. He set the state's line himself rather than waiting. Thin: two acts, no assessment of him by others.

No document dated before 5 March 1861. Foulke p129 n and p146-147 (Cameron's 'quota of Indiana is four regiments and no more', Cameron 'twitting' Morton about the Ohio boats) are all May to September 1861, after the start-class boundary, and Cameron entered office on 5 March. Searched Foulke's whole text for Cameron, OR III-1 for Morton items before 5 March (only the 17 Jan arms letter, which names no one). Nothing reached for Morton on Cameron before the boundary.

No document dated before 5 March 1861. Foulke p133-147 is Magoffin's conference proposal of April 1861 and Morton's replies and the Covington meeting of May to September 1861, all after the boundary. Searched Foulke for Magoffin and the Morton letters in OR III-1 for any earlier exchange: none.

No document dated before 5 March 1861. Their joint dealings (the Covington meeting, the telegrams on the twenty-one Ohio regiments, 24 May 1861) are after the boundary. The two governors both appear in the Peace Congress correspondence of Feb 1861 but I found nothing in which Morton speaks of Dennison.

Chase's own letters, printed from his letter book in the American Historical Association report for 1902 vol 2. To Thaddeus Stevens, Columbus 9 Jan 1861, p295, after visiting Springfield: 'Mr. Lincoln conversed frankly & fully. He is a man to be depended on.' To G. G. Fogg, 10 Nov 1860, p290-291: 'I appreciate beyond my capacity of expression, the sentiments of regard and confidence which Mr. Lincoln has expressed towards me' and 'a true personal friend and faithful supporter of the common cause'. Both are warmer than average. Supported direction: above (not high: they are letters to third parties, one a formal reply).

Chase to C. A. Dana, 10 Nov 1860, p292: 'the overthrow of the Slave Power, is now happily accomplished and the other, the denationalization of Slavery and the consequent inauguration of an era of constitutional enfranchisement, seems sure to follow'. Chase to Henry Wilson, 13 Dec 1860, p293: 'Departure from the original policy of the gov. conc. Sl'y is the cause of our frequent dangers' and 'adhesion to the great principle of separating the Fed. Gov. fr Sl'y' (OCR abbreviations). His own words as conduct (a statement of the policy he holds), both dated before 5 March 1861. Replaces the Schuckers 1874 life as the only leg.

The only pre-boundary leg found points the other way. Chase to Charles Sumner, Columbus 14 Feb 1860, p286: 'I look upon him as a great man, faithful to the cause of freedom & humanity, & worthy of any honor which can be conferred upon him. We don't agree in some views' and 'I heartily honor, & cheerfully praise &, if the Republicans choose him as their standard bearer, shall zealously support him.' So low is not supported by any contemporary document I could read. Caveat: the letter is thirteen months before the boundary, and I found no Chase letter of Dec 1860 to Feb 1861 on Seward (the rivalry for the cabinet and the 'Nicolay and Hay' account are retrospective). If the lead wants low kept it needs a leg from Dec 1860 to March 1861: not reached.

Searched the whole of the 1902 AHA volume (Chase's diary and letters, 1860-61 correspondence at pp 285-295 and the letters to Chase at pp 489-503) for Blair before 5 March 1861: Montgomery Blair is not named in any Chase letter of that period (the Blair hits are from 1862 onward). Same legs and quotations as the regard cell: Chase to Stevens 9 Jan 1861 p295 'He is a man to be depended on' and to Fogg 10 Nov 1860 p290-291 'sentiments of regard and confidence which Mr. Lincoln has expressed towards me'. Supported direction above.

Clay's own editorial in the first number of the True American (Lexington, Tuesday 3 June 1845), printed in his Writings (1848) p214: 'from the defence of our known rights, we are not to be deterred by vague threats or real dangers' and 'Though under the ban of popular proscription ... set on by bands of hireling assassins ... we hurl back indignant defiance against these cowardly outlaws. We can die, but cannot be enslaved.' Conduct, not a self-assessment: he published this while the Lexington mob threatened his press. Also p75 (a Kentucky House speech of the early 1840s, date not printed): 'Bowie-knives, and belted pistols, and the imprecations of maddened mobs, have not driven me from my country's cause.'

Proceedings of the Republican National Convention, Chicago, 18 May 1860: Cassius M. Clay was put in nomination for Vice-President by Caleb B. Smith of Indiana ('the gallant son of Kentucky', p127) and the first-ballot total row reads '101 1/2' (OCR '101Â£', p129) behind Hamlin's 194. Smith, p131: 'there is no one of that illustrious band who are contending for the principle of freedom, who is more endeared to the great heart of the Republicans of this country than is Cassius M. Clay' and three cheers were called for him. Others' judgment of him before the boundary, from a primary convention record.

True American, Lexington, 3 June 1845 (Writings p213): 'The question is now no longer, whether six hundred thousand Kentuckians shall postpone their true prosperity to the real, or supposed interests of some thirty-one thousand slave-holders'. Clay's own conduct as the editor of an antislavery paper in a slave state. The Writings (1848) is a collection of his own speeches and editorials, each dated by the original.

True American, 3 June 1845, p215, answering a local doctor who wrote under the name Junius: 'if nothing but a fight will satisfy this rampant knight of the scalpel, we propose that he supersede this projected civil war by the less heroic, but more harmless mode of the duel. If he slay us, the press shall stop'. He proposes a duel in print. In the same collection p134 a footnote to his letters on the slave trade calls 'The duel with Wickliffe' his one departure from a conservative course 'which I deeply regret' (the document is undated in the OCR, 1841 by context). Own conduct, two instances.

Kentucky v. Dennison (24 How. 66, statement of the case, read in the U.S. Reports text at the Cornell LII host). Governor Dennison, advised by Ohio's Attorney General C. P. Wolcott (opinion of 14 April 1860: 'you have, therefore, no authority to comply with the requisition made upon you by the Governor of Kentucky'), 'refused to arrest or deliver up the fugitive' Willis Lago, and when Kentucky moved for mandamus 'the Attorney General of Ohio appeared, but under a protest, made by order of the Governor of Ohio, against the jurisdiction of the court'. Refusing a slave state's requisition and contesting the Supreme Court's reach are bold acts, done before 5 March 1861 (the opinion of 14 March 1861 is after the boundary and not used). The earlier Appletons point (seizing telegraphs and railroads) is April 1861 and cannot support a start cell.

basis: Same record: the governor's refusal on Ohio's reading of the extradition clause (Wolcott: the clause does not reach an offence 'not known to the laws of the former', and the power 'must always be guided by a sound legal discretion') and the order to protest 'against the jurisdiction of the court' to compel a state executive. The act of 1860 is the state asserting its own discretion against both Kentucky and the federal court. The Foulke footnote p129 is no longer needed.

No document before 5 March 1861. Pearson's Andrew (v1) mentions Dennison only once (p154-155, the January 1861 Peace Conference telegram, 26 Jan 1861) and Cameron only from April 1861 (p224-225 and after: Andrew's complaints about Cameron). Nothing in OR III-1 before 5 March has Dennison on Cameron. The leg the cell cites is dated after the start-class boundary. HOLD.

No contemporary leg found. Read the 31 Jan 1861 Albany speech (1862 pamphlet, and again in the Public Record of Horatio Seymour, 1868, which prints every speech of 1856 to 1862 in full: the 4 July 1856 Springfield speech, the 31 Jan 1861 Albany speech, the 28 Oct 1861 Utica speech and later ones). Between 5 March and 31 July 1861 the Record has no Seymour document at all (the Utica speech is 28 Oct 1861, after the limit). The speeches are arguments and do not show him holding a position under pressure. Near miss: his 1856 speech defends his stand against the Maine law (Public Record p9-10), but the veto message of 1854 that cost him re-election is not printed there and was not reached. The Appletons 'above' stays unsourced for the window.

Report of the Democratic State Convention at Albany, 31 Jan 1861, printed with his speech in the 1862 pamphlet (the report is the newspaper's, printed verbatim): 'Hon. HORATIO SEYMOUR appeared upon the stand, and was received with loud and long continued applause.' (p1). Others' judgment as shown by a party convention's reception, so thin: no individual contemporary assessment of him found. I looked for a national-convention or press judgment of 1856-60 and did not reach one.

Seymour's Albany speech, 31 Jan 1861, p2: 'The agitation of the question of slavery has thus far brought greater social, moral and legislative evils upon the people of the free States than it has upon the institutions of those against whom it has been excited' and 'senseless, unreasoning fanaticism'. He also defends the Southern constitutional claim to carry slaves into the territories (p2-3) and quotes J. Q. Adams that Congress has no power to abolish slavery in the States. Springfield, Mass., 4 July 1856 (Public Record p18 and p20): 'The people of the North are uniformly opposed to slavery, not from hostility to the South ... we have abolished slavery here' but the Abolitionists, 'must go to the extent of interfering with the sovereignties of the State'. His own speeches are conduct that shows the stand, but it is opposition to antislavery agitation and outside interference, not a statement on emancipation by name: indirect, so read the trait as opposition to interference with slavery in the States. The 28 Oct 1861 Utica speech ('Abolition of Slavery impossible' in the Record's heading) is after the start-class boundary and not used.

Mixed record in Hicks's own documents. His message to the Maryland legislature, Baltimore 27 Apr 1861 (REBREC1 Doc 109 p159-160): he 'waited upon' the President in person and 'urged the importance of my request' against passing troops through Maryland, but 'to all my requests I could get but the reply that Washington was threatened', and he ordered Colonel Petherbridge to occupy the Pikesville arsenal 'in the name of the United States'. Baltimore riot, Butler's landing and the railroad all went on over his refusal. His call for the President's four regiments was issued only on 14 May (REBREC1 Doc 166 p245, OR III-1 p190, 13 May: 'So soon as I can get the necessary papers ready I shall call out the four regiments'), a month after the requisition, and was for volunteers. So average is supported, above and low are not. The cell's parenthetical about calling out the existing militia instead of four loyal regiments (NH 4 p163) I could not verify in any document and the OR III-1 p79-80 letter of 17 April asks only that the militia stay inside Maryland.
prior_value: average:NH 4 p163 (he called out the existing militia, mainly disloyal, instead of four loyal regiments)

basis: Hicks to the Mississippi commissioner A. H. Handy, Annapolis 19 Dec 1860, REBREC1 Doc 1 p1-2: 'Let us show moderation as well as firmness, and be unwilling to resort to extreme measures until necessity shall leave us no choice' and 'until the effort is found to be in vain, I cannot consent, by any precipitate or revolutionary action, to aid in the dismemberment of this Union.' His address refusing to convene the legislature (Doc 16 p17-18, undated beside the extract, the Record's Diary places its publication among the events of 5-6 Jan 1861, so the date given is approximate): 'no man of sense, in my opinion, can question' that division would bring civil war, and 'I fervently trust to be allowed to end my days a citizen of this glorious Union.'

The only contemporary legs before 31 July 1861 concern the Peiho in June 1859 and they approve his handling, not rank his skill: Secretary Toucey to Tattnall, 5 Oct 1859: 'Your course, as indicated in your dispatch, meets with the approbation of the Department' (letter reprinted from the Navy Department copy in the Spectator, 2 June 1894 p15, and acknowledged by Tattnall in Jones p109), and Lord Lyons's notes of 10 and 17 Oct 1859 conveying the thanks of the British Government and Admiralty for his 'courteous and valuable assistance' (Jones p106-108). No document of Mar to July 1861 on his Georgia command was found (Jones prints none, ORN I-6 not in the pack's volumes). Supports at least average and not above because the approval concerns the propriety of his course, not his skill, and the Appletons/Wood judgments on 1862 events (Port Royal, the Virginia) are after the limit.

Others' contemporary judgment, printed verbatim in Jones (1878) pp106-109: Lord Lyons to Lewis Cass, 10 Oct 1859: 'the thanks of Her Majesty's Government for the assistance thus rendered to Her Majesty's service by those distinguished officers' (p106), 17 Oct: 'the best acknowledgments of the Lords Commissioners of the Admiralty ... for his courteous and valuable assistance' (p107), and Lyons to Lord John Russell, 17 Oct, that the President said the assistance 'had met with the hearty approbation of the great majority of the people of the United States' (p107-108). Secretary Toucey to Tattnall 5 Oct 1859 approves his course (see competence). Tattnall's 28 Dec 1859 reply (p109) acknowledges 'the Department's approval of my course at the Pei-ho'. A caution: Lyons also reports a newspaper had blamed the departure from neutrality.

Contemporary press and the House, both before the boundary, in Moore's Rebellion Record vol 1. Doc 9 p9 (newspapers of 27-28 Dec 1860): Baltimore American, 'the predominant one was a feeling of admiration for the determined conduct and military skill of Col. ANDERSON', and a Boston paper, 'If anybody ever doubted Major Anderson's eminent military capacity, that doubt must be dispelled' and 'received the highest military commendation in the country'. Diary p11-12 (8 Jan 1861): the House of Representatives resolved on Mr. Adrain's motion 'That we fully approve the bold and patriotic act of Major Anderson in withdrawing from Fort Moultrie to Fort Sumter'. The Record gives the Doc 9 pieces undated (date inferred from the 26 Dec move) and the House date by its running date, the Congressional Globe not checked.

Chandler's own letter to Governor Blair, Washington 11 Feb 1861, printed verbatim in the 1880 sketch p190 (the sketch says he adopted it as his in the Senate on 27 Feb, p191): 'I hope you will send stiff-backed men or none' and 'Some of the manufacturing States think a fight would be awful. Without a little blood-letting, this Union will not, in my estimation, be worth a rush.' His Senate speech of 2 March 1861 (extracts p192, the Congressional Globe not read): 'If we have not a government, let this miserable rope of sand which purports to be a government perish, and I will shed no tears over its destruction.' On 27 Feb he said the people of Michigan are 'prepared to stand by it to blood if necessary' (p191). The letter and speech are his conduct, and not self-assessment. The Riddle and Julian legs are retrospective and dropped.

Greeley's letter 'Slavery at Home', New-York 3 June 1845, declining an invitation to an antislavery convention, printed in his Hints toward Reforms (copy hintstowardrefor00greeuoft, pp 352-357): 'it is not that I deem Slavery a less but a greater evil' (p354), 'Oppose Slavery in ALL its forms' (p355), and on the degradation of the free Blacks 'mainly owing to their past and present wrongs' with a plan that 'would do more ... to pave the way for Universal Freedom, than reams of angry vituperation against slaveholders' (p356-357). His own words as conduct: he states his side on slavery. Caveat: he separates himself from the organised abolitionists and frames slavery widely, so the direction is antislavery, not abolitionist.

His reports as conduct, ORN I-1: ordered 18 Apr 1861 to take the Havana, he reports 22 Apr that he has begun the alterations and on 14 June that the converted ship's battery and crew are ready (p613-615), watches both passes for a chance, and writes frankly on 30 June of the blockade ('the Brooklyn has the speed of me', p618) and on 6 July from Cienfuegos 'my arrival at the port of Cienfuegos, with seven prizes of war' (p619-620). Independent corroboration, U.S. Marshal's Office, New York, 20 July 1861 from two deserted crewmen, ORN II-1 p373-374: 'The Sumter left New Orleans on June 30. The U.S. steamer Brooklyn ... gave the Sumter chase, but the latter, being a very fast sailer, escaped her' and her first prize 3 July. Eight weeks from the order to a fitted ship, the blockade run and seven prizes in the first week support high. Mostly his own reports: only the escape and the first prizes are independently attested (the Marshal's account), and the U.S. Navy officers' letters on the Sumter's search in ORN I-1 were not read page by page.
